title: #65 Make Invisible Steps Visible
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Barton introduces "overtisation" -- a term from his podcast conversation with Kris Boulton -- meaning the deliberate act of making normally invisible or implicit steps explicit for students who are meeting an idea for the first time. His example comes from a diagnostic question on writing fractions as ratios, where a teacher explicitly wrote out that the denominator, 9, came from summing 2 and 7, a step most teachers would explain verbally but rarely write down. He lists further examples from maths -- writing "1x" instead of "x," writing a multiplication sign outside a bracket before expanding it, or restructuring a quadratic to make a hidden coefficient explicit -- all cases where a normally-omitted symbol or step is made explicit. Barton notes the tension this creates: he actively discourages students from using several of these conventions later on because they're "not the way a mathematician writes," yet insisting on the more compressed, conventional form too early is likely to hinder initial learning. He resolves this with a two-stage model: overtise first, when a concept is new, then move to "covertisation" later, once the underlying idea is secure and shortcuts serve convention and efficiency rather than obscuring meaning.
points: "Overtisation" -- writing out normally implicit steps -- makes underlying logic visible during initial learning, even when it produces notation a teacher would later discourage as unconventional.

The distinction between overtisation and "covertisation" gives teachers a principled reason to relax a convention early and reintroduce it later, rather than treating conventions as fixed from day one.
Barton's fraction-to-ratio example shows overtisation working at the level of a single diagnostic-question annotation -- a specific extra written step that most teachers would only say aloud.
The listed maths examples give teachers a concrete checklist of places to look for opportunities to overtise in their own subject content.
quotes: One of the many ideas I took from my podcast conversation with Kris Boulton is the idea of overtisation. Put simply, this means making invisible steps visible to our students, especially when they initially encounter an idea.
He made it super-explicit exactly where the denominator, 9, had come from by showing it is the sum of the two parts, 2 and 7.
Now, most teachers would have mentioned this when explaining the answer, but how many would have written it? I am not sure I would have.
What I find interesting about overtisation is that I actively tell students not to do many of the examples above as they are “not the way a mathematician writes”.
In the initial stages of learning a concept, an insistence upon potentially confusing conventions like these is likely to hinder learning.
Those conventions can be introduced later - a process known as covertisation - when shortcuts can be made in the name of both convention and efficiency.
